newsitem.title: FRANCE: French women ex-ministers plea to Chirac on parity.
newsitem.headline: French women ex-ministers plea to Chirac on parity.

text.p: Ten leading women politicians appealed to President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday to change France's electoral system to provide a greater role for women, who currently hold a mere 5.5 percent of parliamentary seats.

In an open letter published by the newspaper Liberation, the ex-ministers from both the Socialist left and the centre-right said: "Only the president of the republic, by his authority and his institutional position, can impose the objective of parity.
"We turn to him to provide the necessary impulse so that our proposals, which seem the only way to achieve real equality in politics, are adopted," the text said.

Among the signatories were former Socialist prime minister Edith Cresson, now a European commissioner, centre-right former social affairs minister Simone Veil, a former president of the European Parliament, and Michele Barzach a former health minister under Chirac and a member of his Gaullist RPR party.

They welcomed Prime Minister Alain Juppe's statement to parliament last month that he personally favoured a temporary constitutional amemendment to set quotas for women candidates in European parliament and regional elections for a 10-year period.
But they added: "We deplore the fact that he saw fit to limit this measure to elections that use a list system and that he justified this as a necessary 'apprenticeship' for women."
The ex-ministers proposed changing the parliamentary election system to choose some deputies by proportional representation, with quotas for women candidates.
They also sought restrictions on the accumulation of elected offices, which currently allows deputies to combine the roles of mayor, regional councillor and member of parliament.
They demanded that the public financing of political parties be tied to the number of women candidates they nominate.

The ex-ministers also called for anti-sexism legislation on the same lines as a law barring racist incitement and a policy of affirmative action giving preference to women over men when equally qualified for any government job.
"If a constitutional amendment is required to introduce positive discrimination for a period, we favour that," they said.
In 1995, Chirac appointed a record 12 women to his first cabinet -- 30 percent of ministers. But he sacked eight of them in a reshuffle later that year.
